title: PhD Family Visa: Which Countries Let Doctoral Students Bring Dependants — and Who Pays Best
seoTitle: PhD Dependant Visa Comparison: Europe vs UK Family Rules
seoDescription: Can PhD students bring family? Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Ireland and France compared — spouse work rights, maintenance proofs and UK carve-out rules.
intro: Family rules decide PhD destinations. Which European countries let doctoral students bring spouses and children — and what partners can work.
description: PhD family visa comparison: Europe vs UK rules for dependants, spouse work rights and maintenance requirements.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Which European countries let doctoral students bring family — and what partners can work.
content:
A PhD decision is rarely made by one person. Applicants with partners or children weigh a second set of facts — can my family come, can my spouse work, what does the maintenance proof demand — and those facts differ more between countries than tuition ever does. Since the UK restricted student dependants to research-degree students in 2024, continental Europe has quietly become the default destination for doctoral families. Here is the map.

The headline table

CountryCan PhD students bring family?Spouse work rights
NetherlandsYes — standard for employed PhDsFull, unrestricted work
GermanyYes — family reunification for researchersFull, unrestricted work
SwedenYes — spouse/child permits tied to yoursFull, unrestricted work
FinlandYes — researcher permit family trackFull, unrestricted work
NorwayYes — family immigration permitFull, unrestricted work
IrelandYes — family joins; spouse on Stamp 1GFull, unrestricted work
FranceYes — visiting/family permit for spousesFull work after registration
UKOnly research-degree (PhD) students, since 2024Full — but maintenance proof £845/mo per person

Two patterns stand out. Every major continental system lets doctoral researchers bring spouses and children — because European law treats researchers as workers-in-residence, not students. And nearly every spouse permit arrives with unrestricted work rights, which transforms household economics: a working partner in Amsterdam or Berlin can out-earn the PhD salary itself.

The UK’s research-student carve-out

The UK still admits dependants — but only for research-degree (PhD) students, and with the strictest maintenance evidence in this table: £845 per month per dependant, held for 28 days, up to nine months’ worth (£1,023 in London) — on top of the student’s own £1,136-1,483 monthly proof. A family of three heading to a London PhD must evidence tens of thousands of pounds before boarding. Our UK dependants guide covers the mechanics; the summary here is that the route exists, is generous once granted, and is expensive to qualify for.

[[chart:uk-family-money]]

How the continental systems differ in practice

  • Netherlands: the cleanest path — the PhD employment contract anchors a partner permit with immediate full work rights; the bottleneck is housing, not paperwork.
  • Germany: family reunification for researchers requires the standard funds proof and adequate housing; spouses receive unrestricted work access, and childcare (Kita) places, though queue-based, are heavily subsidized.
  • Sweden: spouse permits attach to your researcher permit with full work rights; the practical constraint is the first-year housing queue (our Scandinavia guide covers it).
  • Finland: the researcher permit’s family track is explicit and fast; partners work freely, and the four-year PR clock counts for the whole family.
  • France: the procedure is older and more form-heavy, but spouse work rights follow registration; families settling outside Paris find the costs gentlest of the big systems.

Documents and timing for family applications

Family visas are document projects, and the documents belong to people who may be thousands of kilometres away. The universal set: marriage certificates — apostilled or legalised, translated into the destination language even when the marriage is common knowledge; children’s birth certificates, same treatment; and funds evidence in the sponsor’s name. Two timing models exist: applying together (one appointment, one decision, arrival as a unit) or the researcher arriving first and filing family reunification later. Together is faster when the marriage paperwork is already in order; later is kinder when the spouse has work or schooling to close out — but note that some systems, the Dutch one in particular, process joining-family applications faster when the sponsor’s contract is already running.

Children add two questions parents forget to ask. Schooling: public schools in the Nordics, Germany and the Netherlands enrol non-German/non-Dutch-speaking children with free language-support classes, and places follow residence, not visa type. Childcare: subsidized places (Germany’s Kita, the Nordic municipal systems) cost a fraction of private care but carry queues — register from abroad the week the family permit is granted, not after arrival.

What families should actually check first

Work rights are rarely the deciding constraint — housing, childcare and the salary’s family-fit are. Before accepting any offer: confirm whether the university has family housing and how long the wait runs; price childcare locally (subsidized places in the Nordics and Germany can cost under €300 a month, against €1,000-plus privately in the UK and Ireland); and model the net, not gross, salary against your family’s real costs — our net-pay comparison exists precisely for that calculation. The funded positions below are in countries where the family package is strongest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which European countries make PhD family reunification easiest?

Germany, the Netherlands and Scandinavia handle dependants smoothly because the PhD student is an employee with a salary that meets maintenance requirements. A spouse typically receives an open work permit in Germany and the Netherlands, and children access school and healthcare immediately. Norway, Denmark and Sweden extend full family rights, including parental leave, to doctoral employees.

Can my spouse work while I do a PhD in Germany or the Netherlands?

Yes. Germany grants spouses of PhD researchers a residence permit that includes unrestricted work authorisation. The Netherlands issues the partner an orientation-year-compatible permit with full labour-market access. France and Belgium are more restrictive: partner permits exist but may carry occupation lists or separate job-search conditions, and processing takes longer.

Does a PhD stipend count as income for family visas?

Usually only partially. Employment-based salaries in the Netherlands, Scandinavia and Switzerland meet maintenance thresholds comfortably, but scholarship stipends in France, Italy or Spain often fall short or are treated inconsistently by prefectures. If your funding is a stipend, budget supplementary proof of savings (typically €5,000-15,000 per family member) or add a blocked account before applying.
